items.question: How do you see reliability shaping the usefulness of AI agents for consumers?
items.object: The gap between AI agents' capabilities and their reliability as consumer products
items.answer: Here's the fundamental paradox with agents: the capability of agents, I think, is already in some ways mind-blowing. If agents could do reliably in the real world, in the hands of consumers, everything that they're capable of, it would truly be an economic transformation. But even if they're going to fail 10% of the time, it's a useless product because no one wants to have an agent that orders DoorDash to the wrong address 10% of the time. These are the kinds of failures that consumers are actually reporting.

items.question: Where do you think academic researchers can contribute most to AI research?
items.object: The role of academic research in AI benchmarking
items.answer: When we look at AI, one of the things that I think as academics we can contribute is doing things that companies are maybe not going to do, even if they're capable of doing them, because we don't want to be competing with Google or Microsoft or OpenAI. So I think benchmarking is one area where academic research can really contribute, and more rigorous evals are needed now more than ever.

items.question: Why do you see foundation models as harder to evaluate than traditional machine learning models?
items.object: Evaluating foundation models versus traditional machine learning models
items.answer: As we moved from traditional machine learning models to foundation models, evaluation became a lot harder, because with a traditional machine learning model, it's built to perform one task, and that task is often something really simple like handwriting recognition. So, you know, MNIST is a pretty decent benchmark for handwriting recognition. There are limitations; it doesn't measure distribution shifts, et cetera, but that said, it worked well for decades. But then you get to foundation models. These are models that are supposed to be able to do everything to some degree, so benchmarking started to become really messy.

items.question: What do you see as the central challenge in evaluating AI agents with simulated benchmarks?
items.object: Evaluating AI agents with simulated benchmarks
items.answer: Another thing that makes it harder is when you get from models to AI agents, because agents are supposed to be able to do things in the real world. If you have an agent that's supposed to book flight tickets, you can't actually ask it to book flight tickets, right? So you have to create some simulated version of that. Now you have to worry: does your simulated version actually model reality, or are you encouraging developers to build brittle agents that will do well on your benchmark but completely fail when you put it on a real website? Those are some of the challenges that have motivated our work.

items.question: How do you understand the gap between AI agents' impressive capabilities and their usefulness as consumer products?
items.object: The capability-reliability gap in AI agents
items.answer: Here's the fundamental paradox with agents: the capability of agents, I think, is already in some ways mind-blowing. I'll put it this way: if agents could do reliably in the real world, in the hands of consumers, everything that they're capable of, it would truly be an economic transformation. This is what I think a lot of developers have fully recognized. This is what we call the capability-reliability gap. When you look at a lot of the products that have appeared on the market recently, like the Rabbit and so forth, I get the concept, and sometimes these magical experiences do work. But even if they're going to fail 10% of the time, it's a useless product because no one wants to have an agent that orders DoorDash to the wrong address 10% of the time. These are the kinds of failures that consumers are actually reporting. So that's one thing: the capabilities are really strong, but how do you get that last mile? That's the same issue we had with self-driving cars, for instance. We had really good prototypes 20 years ago, and that's why developers and CEOs perpetually thought that self-driving was two years away. I mean, we're finally there now; Waymo is offering rides to the public in several cities, but it's taken decades to get there. Maybe agents are going to take that long, but maybe we can accelerate that through better rigor in our research and development. There are a bunch of other challenges with agents, but reliability is the number one challenge.

items.question: Why do you find AI coding agents valuable for code that doesn't need to become production software?
items.object: AI coding agents for one-time-use code
items.answer: I think there's a difference between coding and software engineering, and I think that's a big part of where the gap is. For me, as a computer scientist researcher, I write a lot of code, and most of it is not production software. Agents for coding are extremely valuable because a lot of my code is something that only needs to run once, because I'm just testing out some interesting idea that I had. Is this a promising research direction? Even in my personal life, let me give you this example. This is one of my beautiful moments that I had with my kid, which was a positive use case for AI. She's five years old. I was teaching her to tell time. You might be wondering, what does this have to do with agents and coding? But it does, and that's the crazy thing. Engineers always make things more complex than they need to be. This wasn't complex and didn't require any engineering skills. I drew a bunch of clocks for her to teach her how to do it, and she was really enjoying it, but it got tiring to keep drawing these clocks. I pulled up Claude and said, 'Make a random clock generator app.' This is something that I call a one-time-use app. I don't know if there's a standard term for it, but I find myself doing this more and more. It produced the app within a minute. I gave it some modifications, and then I played with her for five or ten minutes using this app, having it generate random clock faces and asking her to tell the time. She really got it; she learned within those ten minutes. It would have been much more annoying for me to have to draw 50 different clocks on a piece of paper, and I've never used the app again. Before AI, it would have been crazy to try to sit down and write an app for this; it would have taken two hours. But now I can do this with AI, and it's not a production software engineering scenario, so it doesn't matter if there are bugs, et cetera.

items.question: How do you think verifiers could help make domain-specific AI agents reliable?
items.object: Verifiers as guardrails for reliable, domain-specific AI agents
items.answer: We're making a bet on what people are calling verifiers. If you have a coding agent, then a set of unit tests is a verifier. You have the agent write code, see if it passes the unit tests. If it doesn't, you can throw it away and start again or give it feedback and ask it to debug it. A verifier is a kind of guardrail. This relates to OpenAI's Strawberry model as well, and other things that other companies are working on. From what I understand, the way that they have trained Strawberry, or o1-preview, whatever they're calling it, is having these kinds of domain-specific verifiers, and then using reinforcement learning. If it didn't ultimately lead to a passing score from the verifier, then that's negative reinforcement, that sort of thing. This leads to a general model that can work well in a bunch of reasoning domains, but it still doesn't give you that 99.9% reliability. So what we're asking is, instead of a general model, if you want to make something domain-specific, only for coding or only for web navigation, can you build really strong verifiers that you can be confident with, with 99.9% accuracy? Can it tell you if the code is correct or if it navigated the website correctly, and can you then use that to build domain-specific agents that can actually work reliably?

items.question: How do you understand the difficulties with making ChatGPT a universal interface to websites and apps?
items.object: ChatGPT as a universal interface to websites and apps
items.answer: Basically, every website or app now just becoming a sort of backend data provider or service provider. I wonder if this is one of the reasons why AI GPT's feature didn't really take off, where they wanted Expedia or whoever else to be essentially hooking into ChatGPT so that ChatGPT would be a universal interface to access all of these. That was an attempt to realize the vision you were talking about: instead of having to build an agent that can navigate the web generally, bring the web to the agent. I don't know; it hasn't worked. Maybe it's on the user side, maybe the user experience wasn't great, or maybe they didn't get as many providers to play nice with them as they wanted. We're seeing that a little bit when it comes to web crawling. As you mentioned, there was a study recently showing that over the past two years the percentage of websites using robots.txt to stop crawlers from accessing them has shot up dramatically.

items.question: How do you see the economic and political challenges of making AI agents work?

items.question: Why do you think “agents” is a meaningful term despite the marketing hype around it?
items.object: Agents as a meaningful term for compound AI systems
items.answer: One might ask genuinely, is this even a meaningful term, or is it just marketing hype? I think that's a fair question. There is a lot of hype around agents, but here's why I do think it's a meaningful term: unless one thinks that companies are going to be able to scale models all the way up to AI, and I don't think that's going to happen, it must inevitably be the case that to take these models and do more useful things with them than they can do just through zero-shot prompting, you have to build more complex scaffolding. You can call it whatever you want; it needs some term. For these compound AI systems, as some researchers call them, which is also a fine term, the more well-recognized term is agents. I feel it is something meaningful.

items.question: How do you think about what makes an AI system more or less agentic?
items.object: Defining how agentic an AI system is
items.answer: We looked at a bunch of attempts to define agents, and it seems like people have a certain set of factors in mind. One: how complex is the environment in which the system is asked to operate? A chatbot operates in a really simple environment compared to a web agent or some other kind of agent. How difficult are the tasks that it's asked to do? Are there multiple stakeholders, whether people or other agents? Is it asked to operate over a long time frame? That's one set of factors. A second set of factors is: is the user basically babysitting it, or is the system given a certain amount of autonomy based on high-level goals to go off and do things in the way it thinks is the best way to accomplish that goal? The third factor is the design patterns themselves. Does it go beyond an AI model? Does it do tool use, reflection, or planning? I think there's no strict binary dividing line, agent or not agent, and the more factors a system has, the more agentic it is.

items.question: How do you think cost should shape the way we evaluate AI agent performance?
items.object: Cost and performance in AI agent evaluation
items.answer: Many years ago, Google's AlphaCode paper showed that if you can repeatedly sample solutions from a code-generating agent, and then you had some oracle, maybe unit tests or whatever, that let you pick the solution as long as one of the generated solutions was correct, you could keep doing this and increasing accuracy. They stopped after one million attempts, but even up until one million attempts, the accuracy kept going up. Starting from a really weak model by today's standards, they could just keep increasing the accuracy. If we don't measure cost, what does it mean to say that you have state-of-the-art performance? You could always just invoke the model more and more times. It's like teaching a kid that there is no biggest number because it's always that number plus one. It's a basic insight, but people were not willing to admit this because it's nice to have this abstraction of a one-dimensional leaderboard. The minute you say it's at least two dimensions, you have to consider cost. It's not a leaderboard anymore; you have to talk about what's the best model for this cost budget or whatever, and it's messy to talk about dollar costs. What we say is, let's plot these agents or models on a Pareto curve: one axis is accuracy and the other axis is cost. Instead of a one-dimensional leaderboard, maybe these Pareto curves are what we should be measuring when it comes to benchmarks. In the last three months, this has become much more common; it's almost become the default way to talk about performance. When someone wants to see if they want to use an agent in a particular application, they can think about their own cost budget. The other thing we say is, if what you're trying to do is get the best performance for a particular cost budget, often the simplest way is just to retry until you get it right instead of more complex methods like trying to debug the code. Don't forget brute force is one of the lessons of the paper.

items.question: Why do you see scientific reproducibility as a useful problem for AI agents to tackle?
items.object: Scientific reproducibility as a target for AI agents
items.answer: We're taking it in a couple of different directions. One is related to whether we can build agents for some very specific mundane tasks that people need to do, as opposed to reasoning, which is very abstract and tempting and sexy, and a lot of people want to work on it. If you've solved reasoning, it's still a little bit unclear what you can actually do with that. On the other hand, let's take a real problem that many people are struggling with. As researchers, our mind immediately went to scientific reproducibility. This is the idea that when someone puts out a paper and code, other researchers should be able to download that code, set up all the packages and messy stuff that's necessary, run that code, and verify that it produces the same results as are reported in the paper. That's a basic prerequisite for being able to build on that paper. Unfortunately, this basic notion of reproducibility so often doesn't work out. It's not because anyone's cheating; it's very rarely that. Sometimes it just takes too long and people give up. It's hard to install a bunch of packages. Other times you have a slight difference in your library version, and because of that there are minor differences in the code that actually translate to substantial differences in the output. It's a subtle problem, and worldwide tens of millions of researcher hours are wasted just reproducing others' code. Our question was: can we automate this?

items.question: How do you design CORE-Bench to reflect the difficulties researchers face when reproducing scientific code?
items.object: CORE-Bench's approach to evaluating reproducibility agents
items.answer: My team got together. Zach Siegel is the first author, and we've put out this benchmark called CORE-Bench. It stands for Computational Reproducibility Agent Benchmark. We sourced this from actual scientific papers, 90 different papers, and this is not just about machine learning; our papers are across computer science, social science, and medicine. Here's the code, and we give it to the agent at various levels of chaos, if you will: everything perfectly documented as it should be, or we remove the Dockerfile that's supposed to be there to make it easy to run the code, or various things like that. We simulate the way researchers often don't do all the things they need to do to make it easy for others to reproduce the code.

items.object: Reproducibility of scientific code in CORE-Bench when setup files are missing
items.answer: They should still be reproducible. A person can do it because they can figure out what's missing and how to fill that in. The code is there. The Dockerfile, the requirements file is missing; figure that out.

items.question: Why do you think reproducing computational research results is surprisingly hard for AI agents?
items.object: Difficulties AI agents face in computational reproducibility
items.answer: I suspect it's hard to pinpoint an exact cause, but I think it's a bunch of things. It requires a lot of back-and-forth interaction with the shell, so that requires very long context. Agents get confused a lot; they forget exactly what the state of the shell is at any given time. That's one difficulty. After you run the code, especially in fields outside computer science, the result is not necessarily in a nicely formatted code output; it's in a PDF. So now you have to visually inspect the PDF using a vision-language model to extract what it has actually output. These are all hard for a model. They're easy for humans, although mundane and time-consuming.

items.question: Why do you see computational reproducibility as a worthwhile challenge for AI agents?
items.object: Computational reproducibility as a challenge for AI agents
items.answer: That's the kind of task this is, very different from some other tasks that are more aspirational, like reasoning. The two main differences are it's mundane, as opposed to some North Star challenge, and if you solve this you're probably immediately going to save people tens of millions of hours per year. We think this is a nice challenge. Current agents don't do that well at it, not well enough to be useful, but we can see that even with some simple modifications to off-the-shelf agents like AutoGPT, we can push up the accuracy a lot. We think that with a good amount of effort, we can get it to a point where we can largely automate computational reproducibility.

items.question: How do you envision LLM assistance progressing from checking whether research code is reproducible to helping researchers make it reproducible?
items.object: LLM assistance for making research code reproducible
items.answer: That's the first step: to be able to check if things are reproducible. The next immediate step after that is to fix things. Once you do the first one, the second one is not going to be that much harder, and we hope this will lead to the integration of LLMs into packaging systems, so that for a researcher to take their code and make it reproducible, you can have a lot of AI assistance for that step as well.

items.question: What mental model do you use to understand how well today's AI agents handle tasks involving a long sequence of shell commands?
items.object: AI agents' ability to handle tasks involving a long sequence of shell commands
items.answer: Not one that I can back up with a lot of evidence, but one mental model is that stuff that's well represented on the web, obviously agents are going to be better at that. In this particular case, I think the reason it's hard is that it's a lot of back and forth. That's not so well represented on the web. There's a lot of shell commands on the web, so if it's a zero-shot thing, what's the command for doing this? In my experience playing with these models, they almost always get it right. But if you have to take a bunch of steps and remember what things look like at each point in time, that becomes much harder. Understanding the state of a file system is harder, and just turn-taking is hard. One of my favorite examples is anytime a new model comes out, I try to play tic-tac-toe or rock-paper-scissors with it. I say, 'You go first,' and it'll say, 'I pick paper,' or whatever, and I'll be like, 'I pick scissors.' Scissors beats paper, and we do this over and over. I keep winning every time. Then I ask the model why I'm winning every time, and it's amazing that the model doesn't recognize it's because we're not going simultaneously. Despite so much smarts in other areas, despite terabytes of data from the web, that's one thing the model is not able to get unless it's been specifically fine-tuned for that. These days models are better at that; I suspect it's because developers have specifically fine-tuned them to understand this. I think that's one of the difficulties of automating a long sequence of shell commands.

items.question: How do you assess the different approaches to improving reasoning in large language models?
items.object: Approaches to improving reasoning in large language models
items.answer: For LLM-based reasoning, there are three broad approaches. One is to just keep scaling up the models and hope that they continue to improve at reasoning. I think that will probably happen if we see bigger models; they will be better at reasoning. But I don't think scaling is going to continue forever, and it's not going to get us to human-level reasoning by any stretch. A second way is inference-time methods, and in particular we've talked about brute-force inference-time methods of using a verifier and trying it over and over. We can imagine much more complex stuff. Broadly, we can call this neurosymbolic AI: the model is the neural part, and there's a symbolic system, whether it's a verifier, a more traditional kind of planning engine, or whatever it is. You try to put a symbolic system and a neural system together and see what they can accomplish together. When we look at benchmarks like François Chollet's benchmark, the ARC-AGI, his hypothesis is that the best models are going to be neurosymbolic. You're using an LLM as a clever way of doing program synthesis, for instance, but then you have to take the programs, run the programs, look at the output, and try to verify the output. That's the more symbolic part. The third approach is what we're seeing with Strawberry or o1, which is actually training or fine-tuning the models to be better at reasoning. There you're using some symbolic system or something else during the training process itself. I think this is a new approach, the first time we've really seen that, and that's what makes it exciting. These are three approaches that, as far as I've seen, are being pursued a lot. I don't mean to say they're the only three approaches, but I think all of them are promising, and it's exciting times for reasoning.

items.question: How do you distinguish the shortcomings of AI agent hardware products from snake oil?
items.object: AI agent hardware products and the distinction between hype and snake oil
items.answer: Almost none of what we've talked about is snake oil. These are researchers and developers trying at very hard problems. Sometimes they fail, but that's perfectly okay. The only little bit dodgy product that we discussed is some of these agent hardware-based products that promised a lot more than they could deliver. I don't think that was because the developers were trying to fool anyone; they genuinely underestimated all of the practical difficulties, the capability-reliability gap, and just how hard the user interface is. Agents are messy enough if you're looking at them on a desktop computer and babysitting them and making sure they don't do things they're not supposed to do. If you have a very limited voice-based user interface, it's a million times harder to get the agent to work reliably enough. I've not been able to get OpenAI's advanced voice mode to come anywhere near the demo performance that I saw. Clearly a lot of hype, but it's not a completely broken product. It's researchers really trying to solve hard problems. I want to give companies the benefit of the doubt here, but I think there have been claims that are much more problematic.

items.question: Why do you find OpenAI's presentation of GPT-4's medical licensing and bar exam results problematic?
items.object: OpenAI's presentation of GPT-4's medical licensing and bar exam performance
items.answer: When GPT-4 came out, OpenAI bragged about how well it did on the medical licensing exam and the bar exam. It's true in a very narrow sense that it did well on those exam questions, but the way this was presented and amplified by the media portrayed a really wrong impression for the public, as if these models were capable enough to take over a lawyer's job. As we know now with the benefit of hindsight, that was very far from reality. Anytime lawyers have tried to use these models in non-trivial ways, the results have been pretty disastrous, like hallucinating entire cases and lawyers getting into trouble with the judge for submitting incorrect information. One reason for that is probably contamination on benchmarks. A more important reason is that lawyers' real jobs look nothing like the bar exam. The bar exam is a very constrained setting, almost designed to let AI shine, and there's a generalization gap between what it's being tested on and what it needs to do in the real world. These are high-stakes domains; errors have a very high cost. Companies unfortunately really freaked people out a year and a half ago. Working in the policy area and on the societal impacts of technology, I saw the extent to which people were panicking and expecting massive and imminent job loss, and not being sure how to react. That's pretty problematic, and that sort of thing is what we call out in the book.

items.question: What do you consider the most problematic use of AI hype?
items.object: Basic regression models marketed as sophisticated AI in consequential decisions
items.answer: The most problematic thing is actually not even in the generative AI space. It's companies using the hype around AI to take basic regression models, just statistics that we've known how to do for 100 years, rebranding them as AI and selling them as something far more sophisticated than they are. 'AI' is used in all kinds of things in hiring, in the criminal justice system, and in various other domains. In criminal justice, these algorithms might be trained to look at various characteristics of a defendant and predict the probability that they will fail to appear at trial. When someone's arrested, there's this risk assessment. If someone is judged too risky, bail may be denied or set at a very high amount, and they might be jailed until their trial, which might be months or years away.

items.question: Why do you find Arnold Ventures’ Public Safety Assessment morally problematic despite respecting the organization behind it?
items.object: Arnold Ventures’ Public Safety Assessment
items.answer: I mention this because Arnold Ventures is an organization that I respect a lot. This is not a company that's trying to fool anyone; this is a philanthropic organization really trying to make the criminal justice system better. They've built the model with really good intentions. The problem is not that they're irresponsible; it's fundamentally that you can't predict people's behavior that well. The intrinsic, irreducible error of these models is very high, so you're making decisions about someone based on little more than the flip of a coin. That's really morally problematic. Even the system PSA by Arnold Ventures, which was developed much more responsibly than COMPAS, had a failure: it was calibrated on a national dataset of defendants, but crime patterns in various parts of the country differ dramatically. When an investigative reporter looked in a particular county in Ohio, or somewhere, where the base rate of crime was relatively low, the model was not accounting for that, and apparently it was jailing ten times the number of people that really should have been jailed. That's obviously very problematic.

items.question: What do you think Epic’s sepsis prediction model reveals about using plug-and-play AI in healthcare?
items.object: Epic’s sepsis prediction model and plug-and-play AI in healthcare
items.answer: Let me give you one more example from healthcare. Epic is a health tech company that's very ubiquitous. They built this model back in, I want to say, 2017 or so, for predicting which hospitalized patients might develop sepsis. Sepsis is deadly, and early detection really saves lives. This was well-intentioned; there's nothing wrong with trying to detect sepsis. They claimed it had an accuracy in the sense of AUC of between 76 and 83. That's pretty high, and on that basis it was deployed in hundreds of hospitals. But it's a proprietary system, so doctors or IT teams in the hospitals couldn't examine these systems. It was only much later that external doctors were able to publish a validation of the system, and it turned out the accuracy was much, much lower, an AUC of 63, and 0.5 is random. This is only slightly better than random. What had happened was a classic error called leakage. This is not Epic trying to fool people, but more fooling themselves. One of the features, one of the variables that was part of their set of predictors was whether the patient had been prescribed antibiotics by the clinician for treating sepsis. The model is making the prediction once it's no longer useful, and they had not even recognized this. Once we realize that the achievable accuracy here is pretty low, it's questionable whether we should be using this kind of system at all. This blew up on Epic, and they had to stop selling this one-size-fits-all system. Now they're just saying, 'Here's our model; go train it on your own hospital's dataset.' I think that's the more responsible way to do it, because every patient population is going to be so different, and there's going to be distribution shift between them. These plug-and-play AI systems don't really work in these high-stakes domains. Those are the more dangerous applications of AI that we call out in the book.

items.question: How do you assess the view that technology moves too fast for politicians to make effective tech policy?
items.object: The view that rapid technological change makes tech policy hopeless
items.answer: Tech does move very fast, and politicians are not technologists. There's a kernel of truth to that, but going from there to saying tech policy is completely hopeless is a very big leap and involves a series of misconceptions. The first thing I'd note is that the politicians we see on TV are not the ones making policy at the level of the details of the legislation. They might set priorities, saying everybody's concerned about AI failures in healthcare, so we better do something about it. But then it's up to the staffers and others to turn that into legislation. Then it's up to the enforcement agencies, a whole different set of entities, to put that into practice.

items.question: What do you see as the biggest obstacles to effective AI regulation?
items.object: Obstacles to effective AI regulation
items.answer: If there's medical AI legislation, the FDA will be tasked with specific rulemaking, and there's a whole complicated process. There is technical expertise in many parts of this system. Maybe you could argue that it's not enough, but it doesn't have to be that senators need to be tech experts. That's not the problem. If anything, it's more things like some of these agencies being under-resourced and not having enough budgets to do their jobs. The other aspect is that regulation is not about the details of the latest models. Regulation is not saying what should your metrics be for GPT-4. That's not how regulation operates. Usually it's not about the technology itself; it's about human behavior around the technology. You shouldn't use it in a discriminatory way, and that sort of thing. In that sense, regulation doesn't have to make any reference to the internals of the models. I don't think it's as hard as people think. If there is political will, if agencies were well-resourced, and Congress were less dysfunctional, we could be doing a much better job. Tech moving fast is a little bit of a problem, but it's not by any means the biggest problem with policy.

items.question: Where do you see the priority in AI policy right now?
items.object: Current AI policy priorities
items.answer: I see a big part of the priority right now as enforcement, enforcing long-existing laws. The FTC, for instance, just last week came out with a sweep of cases against AI companies for misrepresentation. We were talking a minute ago about AI replacing lawyers. There is this company, DoNotPay, that has been making those claims that they've built a robot lawyer.

items.question: How do you see the FTC's action against DoNotPay as an example of what existing laws can accomplish in regulating AI?
items.object: The FTC's action against DoNotPay and enforcement of existing laws against AI companies
items.answer: One of their publicity stunts was saying they would pay a million dollars to any attorney who went and argued a case in front of the Supreme Court by having this robot lawyer talk to them in their earpiece. I think they're bullshitting, because first of all, that's illegal; electronic devices are not even allowed in the Supreme Court. Anyway, they didn't have a robot lawyer, and the FTC went after them and a bunch of other companies for making false claims about their AI products. While the actual action here was about AI companies, the FTC's authority to police these kinds of false claims in the marketplace is 100 years old. That's one thing people miss: there's so much we can and should be doing even without new legislation.

items.question: How do you distinguish AI problems that call for legislative action now from those that need more debate?
items.object: New AI legislation addressing specific harms versus industry-wide problems
items.answer: In some cases, new legislation is needed. There are two aspects to that. One is around the specific behaviors that we want to prohibit. For instance, using image generators to create non-consensual nudes has been a huge problem. It's affected hundreds of thousands of primarily women around the world; we've been hearing so many cases of this in high schools. On those specific problems, legislators need to be taking action. But then there's the big question of what to do about industry-wide problems like copyright, which don't have a simple solution in terms of prohibiting a specific action, and what to do about the danger of catastrophic risks. Those are the areas where there are bitter fights going on. I certainly have my perspectives on that, but a lot more debate is needed before we can get to clarity on those questions.

items.question: How do you think policymakers should address potential catastrophic AI risks given the evidence available today?
items.object: Policy responses to potential catastrophic AI risks
items.answer: Things we could be doing now are insisting on much more transparency from big tech companies, who might know more on the inside about the potential for those risks than we might on the outside. Instead of trying to legislate against risks that are currently in the realm of science fiction, might become reality, but really depend on models behaving in a very different way than they do today, I think the potential for going really wrong with that, curbing AI development for little benefit and not even necessarily improving safety, is too great. While I do support action on AI safety, I think that action has to start with collecting a lot more evidence than we have now.

items.question: How do you think policymakers should distinguish between different kinds of AI risk when deciding whether to act preemptively?
items.object: Precautionary policymaking for catastrophic AI risks
items.answer: There are many ways to taxonomize it, but from a policy perspective you can broadly think of two kinds of risks. One is AI that's used to discriminate against people or something like that. I would say that's not a catastrophic risk. It might be catastrophic to a person who is affected, for sure; I'm not minimizing that in any way. But from a policymaking perspective, we have a very strong presumption that we don't act unless we think those risks are real, as opposed to someone describing in a paper, 'Hey, look, this might happen sometime in the future.' On the other hand, something that clearly would be catastrophic is an adversary taking over critical infrastructure. The reason that's catastrophic is that it's not the kind of thing we can necessarily easily recover from. So it requires action even before such risks have materialized. It requires an application of the precautionary principle. In the US, we're generally very cautious; we don't rush into applying the precautionary principle because we recognize that premature regulation also has a lot of downsides. Different countries or regions of the world might have different approaches. But in keeping with our approach, before we can say this risk is so catastrophic that we can't recover from it, such as bioterror or pandemics that could be aided by AI, and that we should put limits on people's freedom because we're worried this might potentially happen in the future based on models behaving very differently than they do today, to me that's a bridge too far. Let's gather more evidence on that.
